title: Design Food Rating System
description:
# Design Food Rating System

Design a food rating system that supports rating changes and cuisine queries.

Each food belongs to exactly one cuisine. Each food has one current integer rating. A food's cuisine never changes, but its rating may be changed many times.

Implement the `FoodRatings` class:

*   `FoodRatings(String[] foods, String[] cuisines, int[] ratings)` initializes the system. For every index `i`, `foods[i]` belongs to `cuisines[i]` and starts with rating `ratings[i]`.
*   `void changeRating(String food, int newRating)` changes the current rating of `food` to `newRating`.
*   `String highestRated(String cuisine)` returns the name of the currently highest-rated food in `cuisine`. If multiple foods in that cuisine share the highest rating, return the lexicographically smallest food name.

The answer must always use the latest rating for each food. Old ratings left behind by previous updates must not affect future `highestRated` calls.

Lexicographic order compares the first differing letter using `a` through `z`. If one string is the complete beginning of another, the shorter string comes first: `"ab"` precedes `"abc"`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["FoodRatings", "highestRated", "highestRated", "changeRating", "highestRated", "changeRating", "highestRated"]
[[["kimchi", "miso", "sushi", "moussaka", "ramen", "bulgogi"], ["korean", "japanese", "japanese", "greek", "japanese", "korean"], [9, 12, 8, 15, 14, 7]], ["korean"], ["japanese"], ["sushi", 16], ["japanese"], ["ramen", 16], ["japanese"]]
**Output**
[null, "kimchi", "ramen", null, "sushi", null, "ramen"]
**Explanation**
The best Korean food is initially `kimchi`. The best Japanese food is initially `ramen` with rating `14`. After `sushi` becomes `16`, it is the best Japanese food. After `ramen` also becomes `16`, the tie is broken by lexicographic order, so `ramen` is returned before `sushi`.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= n <= 2 * 10^4`
*   `n == foods.length == cuisines.length == ratings.length`
*   `1 <= foods[i].length, cuisines[i].length <= 10`
*   `foods[i]` and `cuisines[i]` consist of lowercase English letters.
*   All strings in `foods` are distinct.
*   `1 <= ratings[i], newRating <= 10^8`
*   Every `food` passed to `changeRating` exists in the system.
*   Every `cuisine` passed to `highestRated` has at least one food in the system.
*   At most `2 * 10^4` calls will be made to `changeRating` and `highestRated`.

solutions.name: Ordered Set per Cuisine
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per changeRating, O(1) per highestRated
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep two direct maps from food to cuisine and food to current rating. For each cuisine, store the food names in a `TreeSet` ordered by higher rating first and then lexicographically smaller name. When a rating changes, remove that food from its cuisine set, update the rating map, and insert it again.

## Key Insight

The set comparator reads the current rating map, so an entry must be removed before its rating changes. After reinsertion, the first element of the cuisine set is exactly the required answer.

## Complexity Analysis

Each update performs one deletion and one insertion in a balanced tree, so it costs O(log n). Querying the first element is O(1), and the storage is O(n).

solutions.name: Lazy Heap with Current-Rating Map
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per changeRating, amortized O(log n) per highestRated
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the current cuisine and rating for every food. For each cuisine, keep a max-heap of immutable rating snapshots ordered by higher rating first and then lexicographically smaller name. A rating change only records the new snapshot. A query repeatedly discards heap tops whose stored rating is no longer current.

## Key Insight

The heap does not support deleting an old arbitrary entry cheaply. Lazy deletion turns old ratings into harmless stale snapshots and removes them only if they reach the top.

## Complexity Analysis

Each update adds one heap entry in O(log n). Each stale entry is removed at most once, so queries are amortized O(log n). The heap may contain old snapshots, so space is O(n + q).

solutions.name: Rating Buckets per Cuisine
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per changeRating, O(log n) per highestRated
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each cuisine, maintain a `TreeMap` from rating to a `TreeSet` of food names with that rating. Updating a food removes it from the old rating bucket, deletes the bucket if it becomes empty, and inserts it into the new rating bucket. The answer is the first name inside the highest rating bucket.

## Key Insight

Separating ratings from names makes tie handling explicit. `TreeMap.lastEntry()` finds the best rating, and the bucket's `TreeSet.first()` applies the lexicographic tie-break.

## Complexity Analysis

A rating change touches two ordered maps/sets, so it costs O(log n). Querying the last rating bucket and its first name costs O(log n) or better depending on the tree implementation. Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Indexed Binary Heap per Cuisine
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per changeRating, O(1) per highestRated
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build a custom binary heap for each cuisine. The heap stores food names, and an index map stores each food's current heap position. When a rating changes, update the rating map and sift that food up or down inside its cuisine heap.

## Key Insight

Unlike lazy deletion, the heap contains exactly one entry for each food. The position map gives direct access to the changed food, so the heap can repair only the affected path instead of rebuilding or keeping stale snapshots.

## Complexity Analysis

Updating one heap node costs O(log n), and reading the heap root is O(1). The maps and heap arrays store one entry per food, so space is O(n).

solutions.name: Square-Root Cuisine Blocks
solutions.timeComplexity: O(sqrt n) per changeRating and highestRated
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each cuisine, store its foods in an array split into blocks. Each block remembers the best food inside that block according to current ratings and lexicographic order. A rating change recomputes only the changed food's block. A query scans the block winners.

## Key Insight

This route avoids both balanced trees and heaps. It trades logarithmic operations for small block rescans, which is useful as an educational middle ground between a full scan and more sophisticated ordered structures.

## Complexity Analysis

With block size near sqrt(m), updating one block costs O(sqrt m), and scanning all block winners also costs O(sqrt m) for that cuisine. Across all foods, space remains O(n).
